title: Safety Protocols & E-Stop
contentStatus: REVISED per Content Principles (60% pass, terminology + notes). Interactive zone confirmed at 2m per DiFacto guidance — treated as current, subject to revision. Alarm pattern reference still pending SME confirmation.

sections.title: Governing Safety Standards
learningObjectives: Name the two safety standards MoRo is designed to meet
Understand why standards-based compliance matters, not just built-in caution
sections.content: MoRo's safety systems are engineered against recognized industrial standards, not ad-hoc caution. Two apply directly at this level: ISO 3691-4, governing safety requirements for industrial trucks, and ANSI B56.5, the safety standard for guided industrial vehicles. You're not expected to memorize the standards themselves — what matters is that MoRo's behavior around people is engineered against requirements designed to prevent workplace incidents, not manufacturer promises.

keyTerms.note: An international standard specifying safety requirements for industrial trucks, including AMRs like MoRo.
A North American safety standard specifically for guided industrial vehicles.

sections.title: The Interactive Zone
learningObjectives: Know the confirmed distance defining MoRo's interactive zone
Understand how MoRo's behavior changes within this zone
sections.content: MoRo maintains an interactive zone of 2 meters around itself, detected continuously through onboard sensors. Within this zone, MoRo's behavior shifts automatically — reducing speed or stopping, depending on proximity — without requiring a human to intervene. This figure reflects DiFacto's current guidance and may be revised as the specification is finalized; it is accurate as of this module's current version, not a permanent fixed value.

keyTerms.note: The sensor-monitored distance (currently 2m) around MoRo within which its behavior automatically adjusts based on proximity.

sections.title: Emergency Stop
learningObjectives: Know what emergency stop does and when to use it
Understand that E-stop is a last resort, not routine control
sections.content: Emergency stop (E-stop) halts MoRo immediately, overriding any current operation regardless of mode or mission. It exists for situations where waiting for MoRo's own sensors to respond isn't acceptable — a person in immediate danger, unexpected equipment failure, any scenario where seconds matter. E-stop is not a substitute for a routine mission pause, which is a separate, lower-severity action. Reserve E-stop for genuine safety concerns.

keyTerms.note: An immediate, unconditional halt that takes priority over all other operations.

sections.title: Operator Responsibility
learningObjectives: Identify personal behaviors that support safe coexistence with MoRo
Understand that engineered safety systems complement, not replace, situational awareness
sections.content: MoRo's engineering handles the bulk of the safety burden, but floor safety is shared. Stay aware of MoRo's general path when active. A stationary MoRo may be paused, not finished — don't assume otherwise. Avoid interfering with sensors, even briefly. This is the same situational awareness applied around any moving industrial equipment, adapted to how MoRo specifically signals its state.

keyTerms.note: Ongoing attentiveness to your surroundings and how they may change, particularly around active equipment.

sections.title: Responding to Unexpected Behavior
learningObjectives: Know the appropriate response to unexpected MoRo behavior
Understand that reporting unusual behavior is standard practice, not overreaction
sections.content: If MoRo behaves unexpectedly — moving somewhere unanticipated, stopping without apparent cause, or deviating from learned patterns — use E-stop if there's any immediate concern, then report it. Diagnosis is not the operator's responsibility at this level. Early reporting, even for something that turns out to be minor, is the expected behavior this module builds toward.

sections.title: Audible Alarms
learningObjectives: Recognize that MoRo uses audible alarms to communicate specific states
Understand that different alarm patterns carry different meanings
sections.content: In addition to visual status indicators (covered in Module 3), MoRo uses audible alarms for situations requiring faster attention than a screen check allows. Different patterns correspond to different states — routine notifications are distinguishable from urgent ones. The specific alarm-to-meaning reference will be added once confirmed against current MoRo hardware documentation.

keyTerms.note: A sound-based signal MoRo uses to communicate states requiring faster attention than a visual check allows.

questions.question: What are the two safety standards referenced for MoRo?
questions.feedback: Correct. ISO 3691-4 covers industrial truck safety; ANSI B56.5 covers guided industrial vehicles.

questions.question: What is the confirmed distance of MoRo's interactive zone?
questions.feedback: Correct. The interactive zone is currently confirmed at 2 meters, per DiFacto guidance.

questions.question: When should you use emergency stop rather than a routine mission pause?
options: When there's a genuine safety concern requiring immediate action
Any time you want MoRo to stop briefly
At the end of every shift
questions.feedback: Correct. E-stop is reserved for genuine concerns, not routine pausing.

questions.question: If MoRo is stationary, is it safe to assume it has finished its task?
options: No — it may be paused rather than finished
questions.feedback: Correct. A stationary MoRo may simply be paused — situational awareness still applies.

questions.question: What should you do if MoRo behaves unexpectedly?
options: Use E-stop if there's any immediate concern, then report it
Diagnose the technical cause yourself before reporting
questions.feedback: Correct. Diagnosis isn't expected at this level — stop if needed, and report early.
